summary: Specifies a base profile for X.509 v3 certificates and v2 CRLs for use with the US National Security Agency's Suite B cryptography. It assumes the reader knows RFC 5280. Its status is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5759 defines certificate and revocation-list rules for applications using the NSA's Suite B cryptography. It narrows options in the X.509 profile so Suite B implementations can use consistent formats.

subtitle: A Suite B profile for X.509 certificates and certificate revocation lists.

tldr.problem: The RFC 5280 certificate framework leaves options that Suite B implementations need to handle consistently. A profile is needed to define certificate and revocation-list formats for interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5759 profiles X.509 version 3 certificates and version 2 certificate revocation lists for Suite B, specifying the allowed elliptic curves, signature algorithms, and required extensions.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5759 is Historic according to the unit metadata. It is an Informational profile based on RFC 5280 and does not itself specify a general certificate system.

today: RFC 5759 is Historic according to the unit metadata, which lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC describes an Informational profile for Suite B certificates and CRLs.

sections.title: Purpose of the Suite B Profile
sections.content:
RFC 5759 defines a base profile for X.509 version 3 certificates and version 2 Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) for use with the United States National Security Agency's Suite B Cryptography. It is a profile of RFC 5280, whose requirements continue to apply unless this document changes them.

The RFC's goal is interoperability among Suite B solutions. A community may define a stricter profile, but communicating communities that need interoperability use the base formats specified here.
sections.plainLanguage: This document narrows certificate and CRL options for Suite B applications. Communities can add stricter rules, but the profile provides a common basis for interoperability.

sections.title: Keys, Curves and Signatures
sections.content:
A Suite B certificate must contain an ECDSA signing key or an ECDH key-establishment key using curve P-256 or P-384. Suite B certificates and CRLs must be signed with ECDSA. The hash algorithm is SHA-256 or SHA-384, matched to the signing CA key's curve.

The profile identifies secp256r1 and secp384r1 as the named curves. An elliptic-curve point may use compressed or uncompressed form, but implementations that rely on the profile must be prepared to process the uncompressed form.
sections.plainLanguage: The profile permits two elliptic curves and requires ECDSA signatures. Implementations must be able to process public keys in uncompressed point form.

sections.title: Certificate Extensions by Certificate Type
sections.content:
The extensions required by the profile depend on whether a certificate is a self-signed CA certificate, another CA certificate, or an end-entity certificate. A self-signed CA certificate must include subjectKeyIdentifier, keyUsage, and basicConstraints. Its keyUsage and basicConstraints extensions must be marked critical.

Non-self-signed CA certificates must include authorityKeyIdentifier, keyUsage, and basicConstraints. End-entity certificates must include authorityKeyIdentifier and keyUsage. A signing certificate marks digitalSignature, while a key-establishment certificate marks keyAgreement.
sections.plainLanguage: Certificate extensions depend on the certificate's role. CA certificates need extensions that identify the authority and its permitted uses, while end-entity certificates indicate whether the key signs or establishes keys.

sections.title: CRLs and Key Separation
sections.content:
The Suite B CRL profile follows the signature rules used for certificates. The RFC recommends that one key pair not be used for both digital signatures and key establishment.

The security considerations in RFC 5280, RFC 5480, and RFC 5758 also apply. The document says that IANA does not need to take further action for this profile or anticipated updates.
sections.plainLanguage: Certificate revocation lists use the same signature profile as certificates. The RFC recommends keeping signing keys separate from key-establishment keys.
